newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open lower, then erase losses.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open lower, then erase losses.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened slightly weaker on Friday ahead of a batch of fresh economic data, including revised fourth-quarter GDP (Gross Domestic Product), but the modest losses were quickly erased.

Revised Q4 GDP, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, is forecast at up 4.1 percent, versus the 4.7 percent growth spurt reported earlier. Other data on tap for the trading session include January existing home sales, the Chicago Purchasing Managers survey and the University of Michigan's final consumer sentiment indices for February.
In early dealings, the benchmark 6-1/2 percent 30-year Treasury bond was down as much as 5/32 before turning unchanged at 97-23/32, yielding 6.80 percent.
Short-covering was responsible for erasing the early losses, traders said, a factor that could continue to provide the market with some support on Friday.

But analysts said the market's upside was limited with the hawkish tone of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony still fresh in participants' minds and the important monthly employment report due next Friday.
Economists at MMS International said the 4.7 percent fourth-quarter GDP gain reported earlier this year is likely to be revised downward.

"The new Q4 data will still depict the fourth quarter as solid, with a booming export sector, strength in overall sales, and lean inventories," they said. "If the data are in line with out estimates, they will support forecasts of a two percent to three percent GDP gain in the first quarter, iwth a two percent gain in final sales despite a reversal in trade."
Among the data the market will get at mid-morning, existing home sales for January are forecast at an annualized rate of 3.89 million, versus 3.87 million in December.
The Chicago Purchasing Managers report for February is expected to produce a reading of 56.3 versus 55.9 in January.
The final February consumer sentiment figures culled by the University of Michigan are expected to read 97.4, versus 97.4 for the early February reading.

At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.07 percent. Six-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.13 percent. Year bill rates were unchanged at 5.35 percent.
Two-year notes were unchanged at 99-20/32, yielding 6.08 percent. Five-year notes were unchanged at 99-15/32, yielding 6.38 percent. Ten-year notes were unchanged at 97-25/32, yielding 6.56 percent.
